Tartak
tär'tak
n. (the second of the two gods made by the Avites in the cities of Samaria)
From Hebrew Tartaq, of unknown derivation. Like Nibhaz its companion, the name has attracted a good deal of rabbinical and antiquarian speculation as to the form of the idol; Scripture supplies none of it, and the dictionary declines to supply it either.

Biblical Definition

Tartak is named exactly once, in the middle of the inventory of Samaria's imported religion: “And the Avites made Nibhaz and Tartak, and the Sepharvites burnt their children in fire to Adrammelech and Anammelech, the gods of Sepharvaim” (2Ki 17:31). Nothing else is known of him from the sacred text, and that silence is itself the entry's subject. The writer of Kings is not interested in describing pagan worship; he lists the gods, states what was done in their service where it bears on the judgment, and moves to his verdict. He will spend a chapter on the reason Israel was carried away — they walked in the statutes of the heathen, built high places in all their cities, set up images and groves in every high hill, burned incense in all the high places, wrought wicked things to provoke the LORD to anger — and he will spend one clause on Tartak. The proportion is deliberate. Scripture is a book about the LORD, and it names the idols only far enough to condemn them.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) has no article for Tartak; in sacred history it is an idol of the Avites in the cities of Samaria, named with Nibhaz.

expand to see more

TARTAK, n. An idol of the Avites, set up by them in the cities of Samaria.

It is named in the same verse with Nibhaz, the other god of that people.

The sacred writer says nothing of its figure or of the manner of its worship.

The Avites were brought from Ava by the king of Assyria and planted in the land.

Their descendants feared the LORD and served their graven images together.

Key Scripture

2Ki 17:31 — "And the Avites made Nibhaz and Tartak, and the Sepharvites burnt their children in fire to Adrammelech and Anammelech, the gods of Sepharvaim."

2Ki 17:9 — "And the children of Israel did secretly those things that were not right against the LORD their God, and they built them high places in all their cities, from the tower of the watchmen to the fenced city."

2Ki 17:11 — "And there they burnt incense in all the high places, as did the heathen whom the LORD carried away before them; and wrought wicked things to provoke the LORD to anger:"

2Ki 17:41 — "So these nations feared the LORD, and served their graven images, both their children, and their children's children: as did their fathers, so do they unto this day."

Modern Corruption

Modern retellings of the Old Testament frequently spend more attention on the religions of Canaan and Assyria than the Bible does, treating them as the interesting background. Scripture's own proportion is the model: name the idol, condemn it, and preach the LORD.

expand to see more

There is a whole genre of teaching that explains the Old Testament chiefly by the pagan religions surrounding it — the fertility rites, the storm gods, the mythologies of the neighbours — until the Scripture becomes a footnote to the archaeology and the sermon becomes a lecture. Second Kings 17 has every occasion to do this and does not. Seven gods are named in two verses, with a single detail of practice attached to the one that required children, and then the writer returns to his subject: what the LORD had commanded, what Israel had done, and why the land was empty.

The principle is one of preaching more than of scholarship. Paul in Athens is the pattern: he had observed the altars and could quote their poets, and he used one inscription as a doorway — and then he spoke for the rest of the sermon about God who made the world and all things therein, and about repentance, and about the man whom He hath ordained, and about the resurrection (Act 17:22-31). He determined among the Corinthians “not to know any thing among you, save Jesus Christ, and him crucified” (1Co 2:2). Tartak gets one clause in the Bible. A ministry that gives the idols more room than that has let the background become the picture.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew Tartaq (H8662), Tartak; 'Avva' (H5755), Ava; chuqqoth haggoyim (H2708 with H1471), the statutes of the heathen; 'asherah (H842), grove, the wooden cult object; ka'as (H3707), to provoke to anger.

expand to see more

Hebrew Tartaq (H8662) — Tartak; an idol of the Avites.

Hebrew 'Avva' (H5755) — Ava; the city of his worshippers.

Hebrew chuqqah (H2708) — statute; ‘the statutes of the heathen’ Israel walked in.

Hebrew 'asherah (H842) — grove; set up in every high hill.

Hebrew ka'as (H3707) — to provoke to anger; the chapter's verdict on it all.

Usage

"“And the Avites made Nibhaz and Tartak” — the whole of what Scripture says of him."

"“They built them high places in all their cities” — the sin the land was emptied for."

"“As did their fathers, so do they unto this day” — the settlement that outlasted the empire."
